arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Mr. Barnhouse argued that possessory and use taxes are difficult to collect.
He noted the city collected only 40 to 55 cents on the dollar.
Mr. Koerner argued that the definition of property depends on prior case law.
Justice Scalia asked why this case differs from established antitrust property definitions.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: The case tests whether a government tax claim fits the legal definition of property. This definition controls the scope of federal antitrust protections.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 25, lines 15-47
Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 3, lines 19-31

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The Supreme Court heard oral argument in this case on November 3, 2009.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 3, lines 7-17

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Hemi Group wants the Court to hold that tax claims are not property.
The City of New York wants the Court to hold that tax claims are property.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 25, lines 15-47
Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 3, lines 19-31

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Hemi Group argues that antitrust laws exclude government tax entitlements from the definition of property.
The City of New York argues that a sovereign's right to collect taxes is property.

sources.label: Official Supreme Court Transcript — file page 25, lines 15-47

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Chief Justice Roberts asked why money is not property.
Justice Ginsburg asked why prior tax cases do not settle the property question here.
